list.listitem: A combination of appropriate history from a reliable informant and cognitive testing is most valuable for determining the need to work up the patient for Alzheimer’s disease (AD).C

Consider neuroimaging with MRI, CT, or PET scan. Vitamin B12 and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels should be determined to exclude other causes of dementia. Add CSF studies if neurosyphilis or Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease are possibilities.B

Cognitive emnhancers provide some benefit. For patients with mild to moderate dementia, donepezil or transdermal rivastigmine are the best initial choice; for patients with moderate to severe dementia, the combination of donepezil and memantine is most effective.B

Monoclonal antibodies such as aducanumab (Aduhelm) and lecanemab (Leqembi) do not provide a clinically meaningful benefit, are very expensive, and have potentially dangerous adverse effects such as cerebral edema and hemorrhage.B

Non-pharmacologic measures for AD, unlike pharmacologic options, are effective enough to likely be considered clinically effective, and should be considered first-line treatment. Physical exercise is the most effective non-pharmacologic intervention to improve cognitive function in AD patients.B

Some atypical antipsychotics for neuropsychiatric symptoms of AD are effective but may increase mortality. Brexpiprazole significantly improves agitation scores in demented patients with agitation.A Case management and other non-pharmacologic treatments are first-line for neuropsychiatric symptoms of AD.
Small benefits have been found with Gingko biloba, tai chi, acupuncture aromatherapy, music therapy, and several other complementary therapies but the quality of evidence is low.B

background.definition: Alzheimer’s disease (AD), as defined in DSM-5: Patients who meet criteria for mild or major neurocognitive disorder; have insidious onset and gradual progression of impairment in one or more cognitive domains; meet the criteria for probable or possible AD and the disturbance is not explained by cerebrovascular disease, another neurodegenerative disease, the effects of a substance, or another mental, neurological or systemic disorder. See below for definitions of subtypes and severity.

list.listitem: 476,000 new cases per year in the United States, as of 2016.
1 in 9 people age 65 years and older have AD, as do 1 in 3 who are 85 years and older.
5.4 million people in the United States in 2016.
Estimated prevalence: 8.4 million in 2030, 13.8 million by 2050.
The prevalence of dementia is higher in non-Hispanic Black Americans (HR 1.5 - 1.9) compared with non-Hispanic White Americans.
In 2015, estimated value of time spent by unpaid caregivers ~$221 billion.
In 2016, total spending for AD and other types of dementia $236 billion.
Treatment delaying onset by 5 years would save $4 trillion after 2010, just in quality adjusted life years saved (assuming $175,000/year).
Estimated total AD costs in 2050 ~$1.2 trillion.
Most common dementia in the United States.
Sixth leading cause of death in the United States.

In an analysis of all medical conditions in the United States between 1990 and 2010, AD showed by far the largest increase in combined years of life lost (YLL) and years of life with disability (YLD) in that period. AD increased combined YLL and YLD by 158%, followed by drug use disorders (85%) and chronic kidney disease (69%).
Idiopathic, increasing with age.
Mild physical impairment on performance-based assessment.
Genetic causes, e.g., the rs1049296 polymorphism of the transferrin gene.
Concurrent Parkinson’s disease.

Prior head injury, especially if recurrent, is associated with dementia, especially chronic traumatic encephalitis. Traumatic brain injury is associated with all-cause dementia among veterans, but not Alzheimer dementia.
Severe hypoglycemic episodes increase the risk of dementia in diabetic adults.
Epilepsy is associated with earlier development of AD, on average 6.5 years earlier.
Persons with prostate cancer, if treated with androgen-deprivation therapy for more than 12 months, have increased incidence of dementia (HR 1.21) and of Alzheimer's Disease (HR 1.16).

Statin use is not associated with the development of a new diagnosis of AD. The same was shown to be true for other agents including PCSK-9 inhibitors in a meta-analysis of 20 trials with 147,441 persons and in a large systematic review of all lipid-lowering therapies.
Of all major cognitively impairing disorders, including AD, there is a vascular component in up to 80%.

In a meta-analysis of over 600,000 participants (mean follow up 73 months), use of anticholinergic drugs was associated with a relative risk of developing dementia calculated as 1.20 - 1.50. However the overall quality of the studies available for the meta-analysis was deemed to be poor.
Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of all-cause dementia (OR 1.6), vascular dementia (OR 1.7), and Alzheimer's disease (OR 1.4)

A recent study showed not only an association between periodontal disease and the development of cognitive disorders, but also a gender association: for every increase of 10% in female gender in a population, the risk of cognitive decline increased by 34%.
Tau protein, a normal component of microtubules, is hyperphosphorylated and forms neurofibrillary tangles throughout the brain.
Cortical neurons, especially in the hippocampus, degenerate and are incorporated with extracellular deposits of amyloid B peptide to form neuritic (amyloid) plaques.

Four common subtypes of Alzheimer's Disease have recently been identified, with somewhat different presentations and affected populations: typical AD, limbic-predominant AD, hippocampal-sparing AD, and minimal-atrophy AD.

Substantial loss of neurons in the hippocampus with sclerosis, with deposition of TDP-43, occurs primarily in very old women: Limbic-predominant Age-related TDP-43 Encephalopathy (LATE) variant of AD.
The USPSTF has stated there is insufficient evidence to support screening for dementia in asymptomatic patients.B

Epidemiological evidence suggests exercise at least three times per week and moderate alcohol use are associated with lower risk. However, 2014 Cochrane review of 12 trials of 8 to 26 weeks in duration (754 participants), concluded that there was no evidence for a cognitive benefit of aerobic exercise in cognitively healthy adults.B

There is strong observational evidence of an association between a lower risk of dementia and herpes zoster vaccines. For the older Zostavax vaccine, there was a 3.5% absolute reduction in the risk of dementia (NNT=29).
Influenza vaccination is associated with a decreased risk of developing dementia among adults with periodontitis, chronic kidney disease, COPD, and CHF.

The Mediterranean diet may help prevent Alzheimer's disease in some patients, as may folate supplementation in bread, and anti-oxidant-rich foods. However, these conclusions are based on observational studies with serious limitations. A diet high in saturated fats and in glycemic index is associated with a higher risk of AD, especially in patients with either mild cognitive impairment or who have a copy of the E4 apolipoprotein allele.
Treatment of hypertension with an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker, or a diuretic, in patients in their 40s with normal cognition is associated with a reduced risk of AD 30 years later.

Cochrane reviews concluded that there is no evidence that Vitamin E prevents dementia in patients with mild cognitive impairment, that no specific treatment strategy for type 2 DM can prevent or delay impaired cognition, and that folate, vitamin B12, and vitamin B6 do not prevent AD.

A "healthy" diet score considering vegetables, fruit, whole grains, fatty acids, sugar-sweetened drinks and fruit juices, red and processed meat, fat, sodium, and alcohol was not associated with the risk of developing dementia among 10,308 participants in an ongoing processed active cohort study after about 25 years of follow-up.
Informant report of memory deficit with functional decline or individual complaint of memory decline should trigger use of one of the screening tests for dementia.

The history and physical for a patient with suspected AD should emphasize medications, including polypharmacy and over-the-counter drugs, neurologic exam, depression scale, and mental status testing.B

Neuroimaging with PET scan, MRI, or CT is recommended as part of the initial evaluation of patients with suspected AD.B New techniques for performing and interpreting MRI and PET scans can assist in the diagnosis of AD; FDG-PET has shown the highest predictive value for AD. B
Vitamin B12 and TSH levels should be obtained to exclude other causes of dementia; add CSF studies if neurosyphilis or Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease are possibilities.B

The Abbrievated Mental Test Score Mini-COG MMSE and MoCA are validated as the screening tests of choice; both the MMSE and MoCA are proprietary. The List Delayed Recall and Category Fluency tests are reasonable alternatives.

Differential.Differential_Features: Sudden onset, infarcts on imaging; no features absolutely definitive; risk factors for vascular dementia and AD overlap substantially
Early visual hallucinations, parkinsonian features, disturbing dreams with agitation, fluctuations in level of consciousness, presence of REM sleep behavior disorder
Early, marked change in personality and social behavior, expressive aphasia
Rapidly progressive dementia, possible prion exposure, positive CSF 14-3-3 protein, increased t-tau/p-tau ratio
Sudden onset, fluctuations in level of consciousness/attention/sensorium

list.listitem: See “DSM-5 Criteria for the Diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease.”

For major neurocognitive disorder: Probable AD is diagnosed if either of the following is present; otherwise, possible AD should be diagnosed: (1) Evidence of a causative AD genetic mutation from family history or genetic testing. (2) All three of the following are present: (a) clear evidence of decline in memory and learning and at least one other cognitive domain (based on detailed history or serial neuropsychological testing); (b) steadily progressive, gradual decline in cognition, without extended plateaus. (c) No evidence of mixed etiology (i.e., absence of other neurodegenerative or cerebrovascular disease, or another neurological, mental or systemic disease or condition likely contributing to cognitive decline).

For mild neurocognitive disorder: Probable AD is diagnosed if there is evidence of a causative AD genetic mutation from either testing or family history. Possible AD is diagnosed if there is no evidence of a causative AD genetic mutation from either genetic testing or family history, and all three of the following are present: (1) Clear evidence of decline in memory and learning. (2) Steadily progressive, gradual decline in cognition, without extended plateaus. (3) No evidence of mixed etiology (i.e., absence of other neurodegenerative or cerebrovascular disease, or another neurological, mental or systemic disease or condition likely contributing to cognitive decline).

A meta analysis of studies correlating either autopsy results or neuroimaging (MRI or PET scans) with clinical and demographic information identified subtypes of AD: Typical AD (T)-55%, Limbic predominant (LP)-21%, Hippocampal-sparing (HS)-17%, and minimal atrophy (MA)-15%. The subtypes vary by: Age of onset: HS < T/MA< LP; Male gender: LP<MA/T<HS; APOE E4 carriage: HS<MA<T/LP.LP overlaps with a hippocampal-sclerosing condition most common in very elderly women; this condition, limbic-predominent age related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE), demonstrates deposition of TDP-43, rather than beta-amyloid or neurofibrillary tangles of tau protein.

In 2024 a working group for the Alzheimer’s Association re-defined Alzheimer’s disease as a disorder of amyloid deposition independent of current or future cognition. However, a subsequent analysis found only weak associations between amyloid deposition and future diagnosis of dementia. The authors determined that between 31% and 36% of the cohort were concordant with the amyloid cascade. They also estimated that between 6% and 52% of those predicted to develop dementia did not. Between 17% and 63% of those at low risk of developing dementia based on the amyloid cascade actually developed it.

The most common presentation of Alzheimer’s disease is a caregiver/family member report of either significant memory deficits or impaired function, suggesting loss of executive function. The AD8 (http://alzheimer.wustl.edu/About_Us/PDFs/AD8form2005.pdf) is a validated questionnaire, administered to the caregiver/family member, with sensitivity 74%/specificity 86% in patients with very early AD; sensitivity increases to 85% with at least mild AD.
Assess patient’s memory complaints and follow for progression.

Perform screening tests for dementia and depression with the patient or caregiver, such as the geriatric depression score, Abbrievated Mental Test Score, Mini-Mental Status Exam/MMSE (best-studied but proprietary), Mini-Cog, MoCA (proprietary) or other tests in Table 2.

A population-based study in Taiwan found the following frequency of psychiatric symptoms in patients with AD: delusions in 30% to 63%, hallucinations in 12% to 26%, sleep disorders in 26% to 61%, anxiety in 35% to 76%, and depression in 22% to 50%.
Mild physical impairment on performance-based assessment is associated with more rapid development of AD.

Physical findings: check the neurologic examination for memory impairment, plus at least one of the four other cardinal cognitive deficits: aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, or disturbance in executive function.
Impaired recovery of blood pressure > 1 minute after standing is associated with more rapid cognitive decline, and with increased mortality, in patients with AD.
In patients with corticobasilar syndrome, failure on specific visual object and space perception subsets is associated with greater odds of having underlying AD.

Individuals with mild MCI and a low MoCA-TS (total score) and MoCA -MIS (memory index score) are at a greater risk of short-term conversion to AD. See for details of the sensitivity and specificity of a range of screening tests.
Short Test of Memory Status (STMS) has been compared with MoCA in multiple settings and tests as well in differentiating dementia from cognitively normal.

Gold standard: autopsy confirmation of neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques in a patient with a premorbid dementia consistent with AD. Note: some elderly have these autopsy findings without premorbid dementia.
The American Academy of Neurology recommends neuroimaging in the initial workup for possible AD, including CT, MRI, or PET scanning.

18F-labeled fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET has sens 0.87 and spec 0.89. Single photon-emission CT is less sensitive and specific: sens 0.80, spec 0.74. MRI has sens 0.71 and spec 0.79; MRI for medial temporal lobe atrophy has sens 0.74 and spec 0.88.

(11C) Pib (Pittsburgh Compound B) and 5 closely-related compounds bind to accumulated beta-amyloid in the brain. The amount of binding, and the pattern of binding, on PET scan can help diagnose AD. False-positive PET scans can occur if the patient has cerebral amyloid angiopathy. False positive scans also occur with increasing age: 5% in patients 50 to 60 years old; 10% 60 to 70; and 25% 70 to 80.

(18F)FDG PET scanning maps cerebral utilization of glucose. This functional PET scan, in combination with software-enhanced analysis of MRI scanning, gives a diagnostic accuracy for AD as high as 88% to 100%.

Findings on conventional MRI scanning including white matter lesion volume, brain volume, hippocampus volume, or all 3, do not predict subsequent dementia better than a risk model that included demographic information.

Scoring systems based on MRI findings can be used to help differentiate AD from other types of cognitive impairment. Of these scoring systems, the ERICA score (EntoRhInal Cortex Atrophy) achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than the other common scoring system, MTA (Medial Temporal lobe Atrophy) scoring: sensitivity 83%, specificity 98%, and accuracy 91%.
In diabetic patients with cognitive impairment, retinal microperimetry, a non-invasive measurement of retinal sensitivity, effectively discriminates AD from MCI.

AD experts are recommending use of imaging and biomarkers to diagnose AD. Individual CSF biomarkers, and ratios of biomarkers, have moderate sensitivity (range 0.62-0.83) and specificity (range 0.53-0.69) for diagnosing AD. Simple studies suggest that adding CSF tests to amyloid PET may add accuracy to the clinical evaluation.

Plasma biomarkers include beta-amyloid and tau derivatives, and their ratios. Abnormal beta-amyloid occurs from abnormal cleavage of the amyloid precursor protein to beta-amyloid 1,42, rather than beta-amyloid 1,40. The most useful plasma biomarkers are: CSF tau,P-tau 181, amyloid beta 42, and the amyloid beta 42/40 ratio.

Paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation is a non-invasive method to detect AD, and to differentiate AD from frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and healthy controls. Accuracy in differentiating AD from healthy controls: 86.5%; AD from FTD: 90.0%.
A substantial proportion of cognitively normal older adults harbor neurodegeneration (reduced hippocampal volume, gray matter thickness and glucose metabolism) without beta amyloid burden.

Order vitamin B12 and TSH testing, and verify depression screen is completed–depression precedes dementia in many cases. Order CSF for VDRL if syphilis is suspected or 14-3-3 protein (in high-risk patients for neurosyphilis or Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease). Elevated plasma cortisol is associated with higher rates of AD with relatively-preserved MMSE (>20), and with AD with depressive symptoms.

The MMSE and MoCA are copyrighted and proprietary, the Abbrievated Mental Test Score, the Mini-COG and the Clock-Drawing Test help identify patients with significant memory dysfunction. All have been validated in prospective trials and found to be reliable. Caregivers can answer the questions on the AD8 for the patient, with reasonable sensitivity and specificity for AD.

The Mini-Mental Status Exam and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) are best studied, and have good sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing dementia, but are copyrighted. The Abbreviated Mental Test Score, Mini-Cog Test, clock drawing test, list delayed recall, and category fluency test have been adequately validated in prospective trials and found to be reliable. Monoclonal antibodies such as aducanumab (Aduhelm) and lecanemab (Leqembi) do not provide a clinically meaningful benefit, are very expensive, and have potentially dangerous adverse effects such as cerebral edema and hemorrhage.B

Cognitive emnhancers provide some benefit. For patients with mild to moderate dementia, donepezil or transdermal rivastigmine are the best initial choice; for patients with moderate to severe dementia, the combination of donepezil and memantine is most effective.B

Non-pharmacologic therapies, while varied, are less expensive, and effective in specific domains of AD care. They may delay institutionalization. with lesser evidence that they improve cognition, activities of daily living, behavior, mood, and quality of life; restraints are less commonly needed. Caregiver mood, psychological well-being, and quality of life are significantly improved with use of nonpharmacologic therapies.B

Physical exercise is the most effective non-pharmacologic intervention to improve cognitive function in AD patients. Exercise improves ADL's, as well as functional independence, while reducing neuropsychiatric symptoms.B
Antipsychotics increase total mortality and may worsen cognition.A
Brexpiprazole significantly improves agitation scores in demented patients with agitation.B

Italian guidelines (2024) recommend against using cholinesterase inhibitors, memantine, or monoclonal antibodies against amyloid for persons with mild cognitive impairment and has nuanced guidance for using cholinesterase inhibitors for adults with mild or moderate dementia. The panel also strongly recommends against using monoclonal antibodies against amyloid for persons with Alzheimer’s disease.

An overview of several common treatment options is provided in Table 1. Several cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine demonstrate a slower decline in cognition compared with placebo, but their effect size for improvement in patient-oriented outcomes is modest at best.

Donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine all are effective for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease for the outcomes of: activities of daily living, behavior global clinical ratings, and improved cognitive function on standardized memory tests.

An individual patient data meta-analysis with 21,138 participants from 80 randomized trials concluded that for patients with mild to moderate dementia, donepezil or transdermal rivastigmine are the best initial choice; for patients with moderate to severe dementia, the combination of donepezil and memantine is most effective. Both donepezil (mean difference [MD] 1.41 points; 95% CI 0.51 - 2.32) and donepezil plus memantine (MD 2.57 points; 0.07 - 5.07) had improvements that exceeded the minimal clinically important difference. For studies of mild to moderate dementia, donepezil significantly improved the MMSE score (MD 1.68 points; 0.31 - 3.06) while transdermal rivastigmine provided a larger (but non-significant) improvement (MD 2.74; -0.68 to 6.16). For studies of moderate to severe dementia, the combination of donepezil plus memantine was most effective (MD 2.49; 1.55 - 3.44).

A network meta analysis reviewed 33 articles on AD treatment--11 articles examining treatment of mild AD with 12 drugs, 17 articles examining treatment of moderate AD with 15 drugs, and 5 articles examining treatment of severe AD with 3 drugs. For all three levels of AD severity, cholinesterase inhibitors were the most effective drug class, and donepezil, specifically, was the most effective drug.

A large meta-analysis, including the most recent Cochrane review, and excluding studies with high risk of bias, concluded that cholinesterase inhibitors are mildly effective in slowing cognitive decline in patients with Alzheimer's disease, and that donepezil is the best tolerated. Adding memantine to the CI may yield a slight further benefit in cognition.

A systematic review found that adults with neurocognitive disorders who take cholinesterase inhibitors are less likely to have falls but more likely to experience syncope than adults who take placebo.

The monoclonal antibodies aducanumab (Aduhelm) and lecanamab (Leqembi) were recently approved by the FDA (despite a 10-1 vote against approval of aducanumab by the advisory committee). An independent systematic review found that there were small improvements in cognitive scales such as the ADAS-Cog, SDR sum of boxes, and Mini-Mental State Examination, they failed to meet the minimal clinically important difference for symptomatic improvement. A systematic review concluded that the most frequently reported harms were amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), including edema (RR in overall analysis 10.3; 7.4 - 14.3; NNTH = 9), symptomatic ARIA-ede,ma (RR for the 3 drugs reporting = 24.3; 9.9 - 59.9; NNTH = 86), and ARIA with hemorrhage (RR = 1.74; 1.2 - 2.4; NNTH = 13). While the ARIA generally resolve with discontinuation of the medication, the FDA recommends a baseline brain MRI and as well as MRIs prior to the 7th and 12th infusions, with discontinuation of the medication if abnormalities are seen. Long term safety is not known and cost is approximately $28,000 per year not including physicians visits, MRI scans and the management of complications.
Two subsequent systematic reviews confirmed these findings of minimal benefit with substantial harms.

The monoclonal antibody donanemab was evaluated in 257 patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease in a placebo controlled randomized trial. The baseline integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating scale score (range 0 to 144) was 106 in both groups, and decreased by only 3.2 more points in the active treatment group. While statistically significant this is not a clinically significant change.
A cost-effectiveness study concluded that neither aducanumab nor donanemab is cost-effective for the treatment of early Alzheimer's disease using $150,000/QALY as the cutoff for cost-effectiveness.

Lecanemab, another anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody, reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's. Its use resulted in moderately less decline in measures of cognition and function, but also resulted in transfusion-related reactions in 26.4% and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (edema or effusions) in 12.6%.
The amyloid directed monoclonal antibody crenazumab was not effective in two randomized trials.

listitem.strong: Medications with slight benefit but limited evidence

list.listitem: There is limited quality evidence of a small benefit for selegiline for memory, nicergoline for cognition and behavior,nimodipine (short-term only), naftidrofuryl (cognition, behavior, and mood), and hydergine for global function.
Vitamin E at 2000 IU/day with anticholinesterase inhibitor may slow functional decline but doses above 400 IU/day may increase mortality risk.
Methylphenidate improved apathy, cognition, functional status, caregiver burden, and depression in community dwelling older veterans with mild AD after 12 weeks of treatment.
A large RCT suggest a slight worsening of disease from estrogen replacement therapy or HRT.
NSAIDs are not effective in prevention of AD.
There appears to be more harm than benefit for metrifonate, receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE), and physostigmine.
A small pilot RCT found no benefit of raloxifine in women with AD.

Optimizing cardiovascular risk factors does not improve symptoms. In a randomized trial of 2,361 patients, after a median of 5.7 years of follow-up, lowering blood pressure with candesartan/hydrochlorothiazide (mean SBP difference 6 mmHg) and lowering cholesterol with rosuvastatin (mean difference 24.8 mg/dL) had no meaningful effect on cognition function after 5.7 years of followup in patients with a mean age of 74 vs placebo.
Neither minocycline or lanabecestat were more effective than placebo.
A systematic review of 4 trials found no benefit of Souvenaid for AD.
A randomized trial found that discontinuing antihypertensive patients in care home patients with dementia had no effect on cognition.

listitem.strong: Insufficient data regarding treatment of AD

list.listitem: Cochrane systematic reviews concluded that there is insufficient data regarding testosterone, SSRIs for depression in AD, valproate for agitation, trazodone, propentofylline, melatonin, D-cycloserine, and piracetam.

listitem.strong: Treatment of agitation and delirium in dementia

list.listitem: A trial randomized 342 adults with AD and agitation to brexpiprazole 2 or 3 mg or placebo. At the end of the trial those given brexpiprazole had a moderately large reduction in agitation scores than those given placebo. Medication discontinuation was uncommon and similar in both groups.

Risperidone and olanzapine both have demonstrated efficacy in decreasing aggression in Alzhemier's disease, and risperidone has efficacy in reducing psychosis. However treated patients have higher rates of mortality, extrapyramidal symptoms, and stroke.

Haloperidol has efficacy in decreasing aggression in patients with Alzheimer's disease, however there is little evidence for its use in managing other manifestations of agitation (e.g., wandering, crying out). It may also increase mortality.

In an industry-sponsored, randomized controlled trial (double-blinded) in 220 patients aged 50 to 90 with the diagnosis of Alzheimer disease and significant agitation, a combination of dextromethorphan-quinidine improved scores in the domains of agitation/aggression, quality of life and caregiver distress more than placebo.
A systematic review identified midazolam as most likely to cause adverse events including intubation in an ED study.
Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube placement is not recommended for patients with AD. Of 103 patients, 54% died within 1 month, and 90% died within 1 year.

Exercise showed the most benefit for cognitive outcomes in patients with AD and MCI. A Cochrane review concluded (based on 17 trials with 1067 participants) that exercise can improve the ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs) but there was no evidence of an effect on cognition or other outcomes.

Gingko biloba slightly improves cognition, mood, ADLs, and global function. However, the benefit was greatest in early trials that were poorly designed, small, and potentially subject to publication bias.
Acupuncture may be effective, but studies are limited methodologically by masking and placebo effect.
Reminiscence therapy studies are ongoing.
A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs with 516 participants found small benefits of melatonin for sleep duration and efficiency.
Computerized cognitive training was most effective for neuropsychiatric symptoms in patients with AD.
Music therapy may improve depressive symptoms and overall behavior, specifically active listening and slightly improved cognitive function.
Italian guidelines (2024) recommend music and art therapy for patients with MCI and mild to moderate dementia.
Vitamin E, plus Vitamin C, plus alpha-lipoic acid or co-enzyme Q were no better than placebo in slowing cognitive decline in a 16 week trial.
Vitamin D is not more effective than placebo in preventing cognitive decline in African-American women older than 65 years who have low serum vitamin D levels at baseline.

Cochrane reviews concluded that there was insufficient data regarding transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), validation therapy, homeopathy, metal chelators/protein attenuators, omega-3 fatty acids, snozelen (combination of light/tactile/music/aroma stimulation), nicotine, thiamine, lecithin.DHA, aromatherapy, bright light therapy, and alpha lipoic acid.

Italian guidelines (2024) provide a long list of popular “treatments” and interventions that are ineffective, including ketogenic diets; aromatherapy; various “formulas,” often containing omega-3 fatty acids, various vitamins, selenium, and so forth; ginseng, gingko biloba, and other herbal supplements; light therapy; acupuncture; laser therapy; and therapeutic robots.
Cognitive stimulation therapy appears to improve cognitive function in nursing home residents.

In a systematic review of 324 reports of the impact of non-drug interventions on quality of life in people with dementia, the best evidence supported short-term group-based cognitive stimulation therapy, which comprises themed activities designed to promote mental stimulation and social engagement through continued learning.
Recollection-based occupational therapy improves cognitive function, reduces depression, and enhances quality of life.
Italian guidelines (2024) recommend aerobic and non-aerobic exercise for patients with MCI and mild to moderate dementia.
Therapeutic touch: benefit is found in severe dementia, i.e., less vocalization and "purposeless movement."

Nonpharmacologic treatments including simple measures such as redirection and distraction are more effective than pharmacological methods at improving behavior. They are first line for behavioral manifestations of dementia.
Multifactorial caregiver support programs in one moderate-sized RCT produced a significant reduction in nursing home placement, but in another RCT, such a program only reduced caregiver depression.
Case management services improved behavioral symptoms of AD, while reducing ER visits and hospitalizations in AD patients.
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) was found in a systematic review of 21 studies to improve global cognition and reduce neuropsychiatric symptoms of AD, for up to 4 to 12 weeks.
Antioxidant intake does not prevent development of AD.
Withdrawal of anticholinergic drugs can improve apparent dementia.
Dementia may be associated with sleep-disordered breathing and hypoxia, but there are no trials demonstrating whether treatment of such hypoxia improves or prevents dementia.
Cessation of a cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine should be considered when they are no longer "clinically indicated."
All treatment choices and care goals should be discussed with the patient and the family, respecting their values and preferences.
Consider hospitalization for complications such as anorexia with decubitus ulcers or for severe agitation.

cell.label: Alzheimer’s suspected (reliable informant reports memory impairment or patient complaint). Perform history and physical, including medications, neurological exam, mental status, functional status.
Any evidence of delirium, psychiatric disease, medical disease, which could mimic AD?

Perform cognitive test such as Mini-Mental Status Exam, Mini-COG, MoCA, Clock-Drawing Test or the Memory Impairment Screen; can have caregiver answer AD8 questions for the patient. Does patient demonstrate both cognitive/memory deficits and significant functional impairment?
Observe carefully over time; at risk for dementia.
Diagnosis of dementia. Apply DSM-5 clinical criteria; determine if presentation fits best with AD or other forms of dementia: Vascular, Lewy Body, or Creutzfeldt-Jakob.
Work up other dementia as appropriate.
Order B12, TSH/T4, and PET, MRI, or CT head.

Consider trial of cholinesterase inhibitor for either mild or moderate functional impairment. Note high cost ($111/month for donepezil 10 q day) with modest benefit. Patients with mild impairment may drive, if they pass the driving test; they can usually live at home, with part-time help.
Patients with moderate diseases should have a full-time caregiver.
Severe disease: treat behaviors with nonpharmacologic measures as possible—redirection, introduction before care, bed baths rather than showers, therapeutic touch/aromatherapy as needed.
Correct abnormalities as possible. Symptoms improve or resolve?
Treat: delirium/psychiatric or medical disease. Are memory and functional impairments resolved?
